title: Formal and informal English
subtitle: depart / leave, mate, I bet, stuff
summary: Recognise formal words from notices and announcements, and the informal words people use with friends.

lesson.heading: Where you meet formal English
lesson.text: Formal English is most common in writing, but you also hear it in announcements, speeches and the television news. Notices, business letters and station announcements are full of it.

examples.text: Only food **purchased** here may be eaten on the **premises**.
examples.note: notice in a cafe: purchased = bought, premises = here

examples.text: I **regret to inform** you that we are unable to ...
examples.note: business letter: = I am sorry to say

examples.text: If you **require** further **assistance**, please contact the above address.
We are not in a position to **grant** you a visa.

lesson.heading: Formal English in announcements
lesson.text: Public announcements at theatres, stations and airports use formal verbs where we would normally say *start*, *leave* or *go to*.

examples.text: The play will **commence** in two minutes.
The next train to **depart** from platform 7 will be the 7:22 to Reading.
Will passengers for Miami please **proceed to** gate 36.
The man is being questioned **regarding** the robbery last night.

lesson.heading: Informal English with friends
lesson.text: Informal language is normal in speech and in emails to friends. A **mate** is a friend, a **bloke** is a man, and the **kids** are the children.

examples.text: *A:* Who's Callum? *B:* A **mate** of mine. He's a nice **bloke**.
I see him **quite a bit**.
Ella's not well, so I'll have to look after the **kids**.
There will still be twelve **or so** at the meeting.
**Cheers**. That would be great.

lesson.heading: Informal phrases
lesson.text: These useful phrases sound friendly and natural in speech. **I can't make it** means I can't come, and **the thing is** introduces a problem.

examples.text: I'm afraid I **can't make it** this evening.
I'm sorry, but **the thing is**, Ella's not well.
What are you **up to** this evening?
I've heard the film is **great**.
My brother said it was **a load of rubbish**.
**I bet** you're hungry. - Yes, I'm **dying for** something to eat.
examples.note: I bet = I'm sure; be dying for = want very much

lesson.heading: stuff
lesson.text: **Stuff** is an uncountable noun. We use it in speech for an uncountable noun, or a group of things, when the other person knows what we mean or we do not need to be exact.

examples.text: Put this **stuff** in the cupboard.
We carried our camping **stuff**.
What's this **stuff** in the blue bottle?

lesson.text: A good dictionary marks words fml (formal) or infml (informal/spoken). Check the label before you use a new word in a letter.

exercises.prompt: Is the word formal or informal?
Match each formal word with its everyday meaning.
Match each informal word with its meaning.
Make it informal: 'I'm sure your parents are pleased.' -> '___ your parents are pleased.'
Make it informal: 'I'd love to come, but the problem is, my mother wants to see us.' -> 'I'd love to come, but the ___ is, my mother wants to see us.'
exercises.explanation: The thing is = the problem is.

exercises.prompt: Make it informal: 'What are you doing this weekend?' -> 'What are you ___ this weekend?'
exercises.explanation: What are you up to? = What are you doing?

exercises.prompt: Make it informal: 'I really want something to drink.' -> '___ something to drink.'
exercises.explanation: Be dying for something = want it very much.

exercises.prompt: Make it informal: 'None of them can come on Monday.' -> 'None of them can ___ on Monday.'
Make it informal: 'We go there often.' -> 'We go there ___.'
Make it informal: 'We should be able to get approximately 40 on the coach.' -> 'We should be able to get 40 ___ on the coach.'
Make it informal: 'You can leave all those books, files and papers on the desk.'
options: You can leave all that stuff on the desk.
You can leave all that assistance on the desk.
You can leave all those blokes on the desk.
You can leave all those premises on the desk.
exercises.explanation: Stuff is an uncountable noun for a group of things.

exercises.prompt: Make it formal: 'We're sorry to say that we are unable to help.'
options: We regret to inform you that we are unable to help.
We bet that we are unable to help.
The thing is, we are unable to help.
Cheers, we are unable to help.
exercises.explanation: We regret to inform you is the formal phrase for 'we're sorry to say'.

exercises.prompt: Make it formal: 'If you need more help, contact them.' -> 'If you ___, please contact them.'
exercises.explanation: Require = need; further assistance = more help.

exercises.statement: Smoking isn't permitted here means smoking isn't allowed here.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Permit is the formal word for allow.
